claims.text: A V–Ti–Cr-based refractory high-entropy alloy with minor Al additions can form a single-phase BCC solid solution.
Minor Al additions stabilize the BCC phase in the proposed V–Ti–Cr alloy.
V, Ti, and Cr are predominantly low-activation elements suitable for minimizing long-lived radioactive activation.
The proposed V–Ti–Cr-based alloy will exhibit excellent high-temperature mechanical properties.
The proposed V–Ti–Cr-based alloy will exhibit irradiation resistance.
W and Ta should be avoided because they are high-activation elements.
Microstructural refinement will improve the alloy's high-temperature strength.
The proposed alloy will possess a refined BCC microstructure.
The proposed alloy will have a high dislocation density.
Sluggish diffusion helps arrest irradiation-induced defect clustering at high temperatures.
Chemical complexity and lattice distortion impede defect mobility and thereby reduce irradiation damage.
A high melting point and stable phases maintain alloy strength at elevated temperatures.
Excluding or minimizing elements prone to long-lived neutron activation reduces radioactive waste.
Above 700 °C under fusion-relevant irradiation, the alloy will retain high tensile and compressive strengths with minimal softening or embrittlement.
The alloy will produce less long-lived radioactivity than traditional structural alloys after neutron exposure.
Reduced-activation ferritic/martensitic steels may perform less well than the proposed HEA under extreme high-temperature irradiation conditions.
Contamination by higher-activation elements could compromise the alloy's low-activation performance.
At sufficiently high irradiation doses, sluggish-diffusion and defect-recombination benefits may cease to be effective.
Defect recombination and microstructural stability mechanisms are well established in HEAs.
The long-term irradiation response and activation behavior of the proposed V–Ti–Cr composition remain experimentally unvalidated.
